In Which the Universe Refuses to Behave
The murder had not happened yet.
This was, in itself, not especially alarming. Most murders have the decency to wait until after they happen before becoming administrative problems.
The difficulty was that the Relativistic Investigation Bureau had already received the paperwork.
The time of death had been entered.
He was also, regrettably, the sort of man who noticed discrepancies in official paperwork.
This particular discrepancy was rather difficult to ignore.
The paperwork predicted his death three days before it was due to occur.
Derek therefore did what any sensible investigator would do.
Then the clock again, because the first check had produced a result he found professionally inconvenient.
It had stopped at precisely the time printed on the murder notice.
This would have been an excellent reason to panic if Derek had not already spent several years working in physics.
Physicists are trained to distrust coincidences, measurements, clocks, diagrams, intuition and, when necessary, each other.
They are particularly suspicious of anything described as obvious.
This suspicion has served the profession rather well.
Newton discovered that falling objects obeyed laws.
Einstein discovered that space and time did not behave the way Newton had imagined.
General Relativity then made the still more inconvenient suggestion that gravity is deeply connected to the geometry of spacetime itself.
None of this would have been especially troublesome if the universe had confined its eccentricities to respectable laboratories.
Clocks could disagree about elapsed time without either clock being broken.
Distances could depend on the observer.
Two observers could disagree about whether separated events were simultaneous.
The speed of light could remain the same for all inertial observers.
Gravity could alter the rate at which clocks accumulated proper time.
Curvature could reveal itself through the behaviour of neighbouring free-fall paths.
And somewhere along the way, a cucumber became relevant.
The universe had simply been uncooperative.
That was how the Relativistic Investigation Bureau came into existence.
It was not founded because anyone had dreamed of becoming a civil servant.
Nobody dreams of becoming a civil servant.

Bureaux involve stationery, regulations, meetings, filing systems and the possibility that a perfectly respectable physical anomaly may be rejected because Form 17B was completed in black ink instead of blue.
The Bureau existed because Derek Gent had begun asking questions.
Unfortunately, Derek was very good at asking them.
There was Trevor Boltzman, who understood difficult mathematics but occasionally required a small verbal shove toward the obvious.
There was Penny Gent, who could make tensor calculus sound almost reasonable and who regarded most forms of nonsense as a personal challenge.
There was Julius Barbarian, who maintained that time did not exist and had developed an argument for this that was considerably more coherent than anyone wanted it to be.
There was Hermann Minkowski, who regarded spacetime as an entirely adequate explanation of itself and had no patience with people who demanded that it behave more intuitively.

And there was Alfred Weinstein, who had somehow acquired the inconvenient habit of being the real inventor of Special and General Relativity in a universe where history insisted on crediting Einstein.
Weinstein regarded this as plagiarism on a cosmological scale.
He had attempted to correct the historical record through ordinary academic channels.
The academic channels had requested Form 17B.
Sherlock was also, according to Penny, the least improbable member of the Bureau once one had properly understood General Relativity.
Nobody asked him to explain this.
The Bureau had learned that explanations often made matters worse.

So when Derek found a murder notice announcing his own future death, he did not immediately conclude that he was being hunted by a time traveller, a quantum ghost or an unusually vindictive railway timetable.
A murder that had not happened.
There was only one sensible response.
Because if the universe has made a mistake, someone has to fill in the form.
The Murder That Hadn't Happened Yet
At precisely 9:17 on a Tuesday morning, Derek Gent received an email informing him that he was dead.
Derek had always suspected that death would arrive by email.

Not because he was especially pessimistic, but because nearly everything important seemed to arrive by email these days. Electricity bills. Insurance renewals. Invitations to webinars. Notifications that someone had changed a password Derek had never used.
Death was simply the logical next step.
What surprised him was the sender.
The message had come from the Derek Gent Relativistic Investigation Bureau.
The Bureau was not supposed to send him emails.

More precisely, it was a small private investigative organization occupying two rooms on the second floor of an old office building in London, plus a corridor which the landlord insisted was a communal area and Derek insisted belonged to the Bureau whenever he needed somewhere to put a coat.
The Bureau dealt primarily with unusual cases.
This was partly because Derek liked unusual cases and partly because ordinary cases paid terribly.
The sign on the frosted glass door read:
And underneath that, added by Penny Gent several years earlier:
NO MURDERS BEFORE 10 A.M. WITHOUT AN APPOINTMENT
Penny Gent had pointed out that they had never actually received a murder before ten.
Derek had remarked that this was beside the point.
Penny Gent had remarked that was precisely the point.
He was now looking at an email from the Bureau.
We regret to inform you that you have been murdered.
The incident will occur tomorrow at 11:03 a.m.
He looked at the sender's address.
He looked at the Bureau's computer.
Everything appeared to be where it ought to be.
The kettle was where the kettle normally was, which was not necessarily where it ought to be.
Nothing appeared to have been disturbed.
Derek looked at the email again.
Across the room, Trevor Boltzman looked up.
Trevor was twenty-eight, highly intelligent, technically qualified, and possessed of the unfortunate tendency to think about one problem at a time.
This made him very good at mathematics.
It made him considerably less useful when confronted with a sentence such as:
"You're telling me you've been murdered tomorrow?"
Trevor put his glasses back on.
"I wasn't sure what else to say."
"Trevor, I have been working in this field for twenty-three years."
"I know the difference between something being impossible and something being highly inconvenient."
Trevor nodded and walked toward the kitchen.
There was a knock at the door.
Before Derek could answer, the door opened.
She was also one of those people who appeared to have been designed specifically to make other people lose their train of thought.
She was a striking brunette, though Derek had never used the word striking in her presence because he valued his life and had no wish to become the subject of a police report.
She wore a dark coat, carried a handbag, and had the calm expression of someone who had already dealt with several irritating people before breakfast.
"Like you've just discovered the Inland Revenue has found you."
She walked over to the computer.
Derek turned the monitor toward her.
Unlike Trevor, who approached every new piece of information as if it might require a spreadsheet, Penny Gent seemed to absorb things almost before anyone had spoken.
"I'd hate to think you'd become predictable."
Trevor came back carrying three mugs.
Trevor handed Penny Gent her mug.
"I thought there were only two of us."
"She's been here for approximately ninety seconds."
"And yet somehow you've already forgotten that she exists."
Derek turned back to the computer.
The murder was, in some respects, straightforward.
Derek stopped breathing for a moment.
Derek turned the monitor toward them.
The photograph showed the Bureau office.
Not a room that resembled it.
The same window overlooking the street.
The same framed photograph of Derek's grandfather standing beside a Morris Minor in 1964.
And on the floor, face-down beside the desk, was Derek.
There was blood on the back of his shirt.
"Because it would be a very poor photograph if I didn't."
A small brass railway clock stood beside the computer.
He looked at the clock on his own desk.
He looked back at the photograph.
"And the photograph was apparently taken at the moment of my death."
"Trevor, if you are going to work here, you really must learn to recognize the moment when a mystery is standing on the table waving its arms."
"If it's a photograph taken tomorrow, then why does the clock show eleven-oh-three?"
"So the photograph was taken two hours later."
Derek stood and walked to the window.
Outside, London was doing what London did best.
"Do you know what the irritating thing about this is?"
Trevor immediately reconsidered his life choices.
"Everyone assumes time is the same everywhere."
"Because Alfred Weinstein ruined that particular assumption."
Derek picked up a marker and went to the whiteboard.
"Suppose you're standing on a platform and a train passes you at a very high speed."
"Lightning strikes the front and rear of the train simultaneously."
"An observer standing on the platform, exactly halfway between the two strikes, sees the flashes arrive simultaneously."
"Now imagine someone sitting exactly halfway between the front and rear of the train."
"So the passenger is moving toward the flash at the front and away from the flash at the back."
"But the lightning still struck at the same time."
"Different observers can disagree about whether two separated events happened at the same time."
Penny Gent looked at the photograph.
"And the timestamp is an observation of that event."
"So we need to know the reference frame."
"Wouldn't the photograph itself give us the frame?"
"Light takes time to reach the camera."
Derek could see the thought arriving.
"So even the photograph isn't necessarily showing us what happened when we think it happened."
There was something in the lower-right corner.
The railway clock in the photograph wasn't showing exactly 11:03.
He looked at his own clock.
"Because if this were simply a badly set clock, there's no reason for the seconds to line up."
Derek opened the Bureau's internal records.
The system showed no record of the brass clock.
Derek searched the building's security footage.
The shadow moved normally as the light from the window changed.
"So how do we know anything is real?"
He took the brass clock from the photograph and compared its mechanism with the Bureau's clocks.
Derek turned the photograph upside down.
There was a small number written on the back.
He looked at the case database.
Then the computer made a noise.
The case contained only three pieces of information.
DO NOT LET TREVOR NEAR THE CLOCK.
"Someone—or something—is creating cases inside our system."
Derek turned the monitor toward them.
"So someone is doing it from here."
Penny Gent looked around the room.
There were three people in it.
Derek looked at the three chairs.
"Or one of us hasn't done it yet."
All three looked at the screen.
Penny Gent walked to the window.
He looked at the case file.
"Before we worry about who did it, we need to know what actually happened."
"Then we're going to need to leave."
"So whoever put it here expected us to find it."
"To the place where it came from."
On the back, beneath the number 1047, another line had appeared.
"So how are we supposed to investigate it?"
"How do we know we'll get there?"
"Because someone has already told us that we will."
"Then we'll have wasted a perfectly good morning."
"Then I suppose I'll have to solve my own murder."
Inside the empty office, the brass clock appeared on Derek's desk.
But now the clock was showing 11:03.
And outside the office, somewhere far away, a train whistle sounded.
There was no railway station anywhere near the building.
The Bureau's computer switched itself on.
And beneath it, in smaller letters:
DO NOT LET WEINSTEIN GET TO THE STATION FIRST.
Then the computer displayed the date.
By Wednesday morning, Derek Gent had decided that there were two kinds of impossible.
The first kind was the ordinary sort.
A man could not be in two places at once.
A photograph could not normally exist before it was taken.
A clock could not run backwards without either being broken or being subjected to a level of engineering that Derek considered unnecessarily ambitious.
The second kind was considerably worse.
The second kind was something that was perfectly consistent with the laws of physics but completely inconsistent with common sense.
Derek had spent most of his professional life dealing with the second kind.
He found it much more expensive.
At 8:36 on Wednesday morning, he was standing in front of the whiteboard in the Bureau while Trevor sat at the desk and Penny Gent leaned against the window.
The brass railway clock sat between them.
It had arrived sometime during the night.
Nobody knew where it had come from.
Derek had written three words on the board.
"The first thing we need to establish," he remarked, "is what actually happened."
Penny Gent looked at the clock.
"We have a photograph of you lying dead."
"We have a second timestamp in the Bureau."
"Because we don't know whether they are supposed to agree."
He labelled one A and the other B.
"These happen somewhere in spacetime. We can describe each event by four coordinates."
"And different observers can assign different coordinates."
"Because they're moving relative to one another."
Penny Gent looked at the photograph.
"So the question isn't simply when Derek died."
"It's when Derek died according to which observer."
"But the death itself either happened or it didn't."
"That part doesn't depend on the observer."
Penny Gent picked up the photograph.
"Because light has to travel from the event to the camera."
"So the photograph doesn't show the event itself."
"It shows light arriving from the event."
"Which means the image contains information about an earlier event."
"So when we say the photograph was taken at 11:03, we're already making an assumption about the relationship between the clock and the event."
Derek walked to the desk and picked up the brass clock.
There was a small metal plate on the back.
"More precise than it has any right to be."
Derek took the clock from him.
There was nowhere to put anything substantial.
Penny Gent looked at the photograph.
"So seventeen is part of the message."
"Seventeen kilometres per second. Seventeen percent of something. Seventeen metres per second. There's no shortage of seventeen in physics."
Trevor looked at the clock again.
Trevor realized he had remarked something interesting.
"If seventeen seconds is a proper-time interval..."
"Then we'd need to know which worldline we're talking about," Penny Gent remarked.
Derek looked at both of them.
"Which means we're already getting ahead of ourselves."
"We need the simplest possible explanation first."
"Do you ever find it strange saying that?"
"That you're using Weinstein's equations to investigate a case involving Weinstein's own theory."
"Because if you want to investigate a crime involving gravity, you use General Relativity."
"If you want to investigate a crime involving relative motion and time, you use Special Relativity."
"Then you start charging by the hour."
Derek pointed to the first equation.
"And the important bit is that t' depends on x."
"Meaning that time in one frame depends partly on where the event occurs in the other frame."
"So two events that are simultaneous in one frame need not be simultaneous in another."
Penny Gent remarked, "Which is relativity of simultaneity."
Derek looked at the photograph again.
"And that is the first thing I want to test."
He opened the Bureau's analysis software.
"Suppose the photograph corresponds to an actual event tomorrow at 11:03:17."
"And suppose the camera and the Bureau are moving relative to one another."
"Then the time coordinate assigned to that event could be different in the two frames."
Trevor remarked, "But unless they're moving at a substantial fraction of the speed of light, the difference should be tiny."
"Small enough that London Underground timetables are generally a greater source of temporal uncertainty."
"So ordinary motion can't explain a difference of nearly two hours."
"So Special Relativity is telling us the premise is wrong."
"Could the photograph be showing a different event?"
"The photograph may be real, but we assume it shows Derek's death."
"What if it shows Derek at a different event that happens to look like his death?"
"That would be rather unfortunate for Derek."
"So we don't actually know that the photograph is evidence of murder."
"Then why did you say you'd been murdered?"
Penny Gent remarked, "We're going to need to question the Bureau."
"I understand you have been using the Lorentz transformation."
"Are you telling me I don't understand Special Relativity?"
"I'm telling you that you are trying to make a flat-spacetime transformation solve a problem that may not be flat."
Derek looked at the brass railway clock.
"In a patent attorney's office in Schwabing."
"He has been thinking about General Relativity."
"Because Alfred has just discovered that the clocks in his office are disagreeing."
"Are you saying the clocks in Munich and London are showing the same relativistic anomaly?"
"I'm saying that if you transform the measurements into a common frame, they are related."
"Because Alfred wants to speak to you."
"I've been told you have a clock."
"No. You have a very specific problem."
"Are you saying you have already seen the clock?"
"I am very old, Mr Gent, but I am not senile."
"The interesting thing is that I remember seeing it."
Penny Gent took a slow breath.
Trevor looked as though he would quite like to leave the country.
"Could it have been a relativistic effect?"
"Could the photograph have been from another frame?"
"Could the event be displaced in time?"
"Could I have been dead in one frame and alive in another?"
"You could be dead according to one description of an event and alive according to another if we're actually talking about different events."
"Which means the photograph may be telling you the truth."
Minkowski's voice came faintly from the background.
Penny Gent's expression had gone completely serious.
Trevor was standing beside the whiteboard.
Penny Gent looked at the ceiling.
"How can you be alive and dead at the same time?"
"He Derek remarked was alive and dead."
Penny Gent walked to the whiteboard.
"Not if the transformation requires a velocity greater than light."
"Then perhaps the events are not connected the way we assume."
"Because Alfred Weinstein doesn't make mistakes with relativity."
"He might misunderstand an unfamiliar physical phenomenon."
"So if Weinstein reads the clock is showing us two different events rather than one event seen from two frames..."
Derek looked at the brass clock.
"Because the clock isn't telling us where to go."
The letters LGV were still stamped into the back.
Trevor looked at the clock face.
A new case file had appeared.
Derek stared at the last line.
"Because the Bureau is telling us which frame to use."
"And it has chosen an inertial frame."
"So perhaps General Relativity isn't involved after all."
For the first time since receiving the murder notice, he felt genuinely cheerful.
The future appeared to have leaked into the present.
And Alfred Weinstein was apparently going to witness Derek's death tomorrow while Derek remained alive today.
In other words, it was exactly the sort of case for which the Bureau existed.
Penny Gent picked up her handbag.
Trevor looked at the brass clock.
"This one appears to be an exception."
He looked back through the glass.
For just a moment, he thought he saw somebody sitting at his desk.
The brass clock was in his hand.
He looked at the chair again.
Penny Gent appeared in the doorway.
As the door closed, the computer screen came on by itself.
Derek looked at the brass clock.
And somewhere, very far away—or possibly very close—the sound of a train began to move through the walls.
By Thursday morning, Alfred Weinstein was sitting in a patent attorney's office in Schwabing.
The patent attorney was explaining a device intended to improve the efficiency of a mechanical regulator.
Weinstein had been listening for approximately six minutes.
He had understood the first two.
The fourth had involved a spring.
The fifth had involved a spring behaving in a way Weinstein considered personally insulting.
By the sixth minute, his mind had left the room.
He looked out of the window.
A cyclist narrowly avoided a delivery cart.
A dog had apparently decided that the entire afternoon belonged to it.
Weinstein watched the movement for a while.
Then he looked at the clock.
He had been in the office for forty-three minutes.
The feeling of time passing was obviously psychological.
He looked at the clock again.
One clock was on the wall.
His watch was on his wrist.
Then his mind wandered back to the clocks.
Suppose two identical clocks were placed at different heights.
General Relativity predicted that a clock deeper in a gravitational field would run more slowly than one higher up.
The difference under ordinary circumstances was extremely small.
And, more importantly, it was measurable.
On the margin of the patent application he wrote:
GRAVITY CHANGES THE RATE OF TIME.
Weinstein looked at the drawing for a moment.
“Because you've assumed the temperature remains constant.”
Weinstein turned the paper around and pointed to a line.
The attorney leaned over the desk.
The patent attorney looked at the amended diagram.
Weinstein looked at his watch again.
The difference between it and the wall clock had increased.
The attorney pointed towards the secretary's desk.
He compared it with his watch.
Then he looked at the positions of all three.
The difference was far too large.
The secretary looked at the clocks.
Then looked at his watch again.
“I thought you didn't believe in impossible things.”
“What about the rest of the patent?”
“It will continue being wrong while I'm gone.”
Hermann Minkowski was standing in the corridor.
“That is what Derek Gent is trying to discover.”
A man was lying face-down on the floor.
Weinstein looked at the photograph again.
“And you expect me to believe this?”
He looked at the clock in the photograph.
“The timestamp alone tells us almost nothing.”
“And the light-travel time between the event and the camera.”
The same clock he'd seen in his office.
“You have an unfortunate tendency to turn information into puzzles.”
“It's much too large to be explained by the gravitational field of the Earth at that height.”
“...or we're not dealing with the Earth's ordinary gravitational field.”
In London, Derek Gent was standing in the Bureau, staring at the same photograph.
The three of them had spent the morning testing the Lorentz transformation against the mysterious timestamps.
Derek looked at the latest calculation.
“The relative velocity required to transform the two timestamps is greater than the speed of light.”
“So the two timestamps cannot simply be the same event described in two inertial frames.”
“Then one of our assumptions is wrong.”
Penny Gent looked at the photograph.
“Could the photograph be genuine but the event misidentified?”
“Could the clock be genuine but the frame wrong?”
“Could both be genuine and there be another effect?”
“Could a strong gravitational field do it?”
“Not unless the landlord has installed a neutron star.”
Penny Gent looked at the floor.
“No. I mean I have seen that exact clock.”
Derek glanced at the brass clock.
“That depends on which time you mean.”
“Alfred, do you know what causes the effect?”
“I am not there to solve your case.”
“Then why are you coming to London?”
Derek looked at the brass clock.
“Does General Relativity explain what we're seeing?”
“The gravitational time-dilation effect is real. We understand it extremely well. What we don't understand is why your clocks are showing a difference so large.”
“We're applying known relativity to an unknown situation.”
Penny Gent picked up her coat.
Derek picked up the brass clock.
Penny Gent paused at the door.
The initials LGV were still stamped into the back.
“I want to know what this means.”
Derek put the clock in his coat pocket.
Behind them, the computer switched itself on.
In Munich, at almost exactly the same moment, the wall clock in the patent attorney's office stopped.
Behind them, in the patent attorney's office, the clock started again.
Only this time it was running backwards.
The Man Who Had Mislaid Time
Julius Barbarian lived in a house which appeared to have been designed by someone who had once been told what a house was and had then decided to improvise.
It stood on a quiet street in Munich, behind a low wall and a hedge which had clearly given up several years earlier.
There was no sign on the gate.
There was, however, a small brass plaque beside the front door.
"He's going to be one of those people."
Penny Gent looked at the plaque.
Trevor stood behind them, holding the brass clock.
"The sort who put philosophical statements on doorways."
He pressed it a third time.

Julius Barbarian was in his late sixties, perhaps early seventies. He was slim, silver-haired, and dressed in a dark jacket, open-necked shirt and rather expensive-looking trousers that had nevertheless acquired a small stain of something orange.
"How did you know who we were?"
Not piles of papers, as in an ordinary untidy office.
Rather, papers appeared to have been distributed according to some private mathematical principle which Barbarian alone understood.
There were books on physics, philosophy, mathematics and cosmology.
There were also several books about gardening.
One shelf contained nothing but clocks.
There were perhaps twenty of them.
"I collect things people use to pretend time exists."
He walked into the sitting room.
A large wooden table occupied the centre of the room.
Then Barbarian looked directly at Weinstein.
Weinstein, who had been examining a book on the shelf, turned.
"You've spent most of your life making time behave."
"I've spent most of my life making physicists stop treating it as obvious."
"We have clocks that appear to disagree by an amount that cannot be explained by ordinary gravitational time dilation."
"And the same anomaly appears in London and Munich."
"And the clocks appear to be connected to an event which hasn't happened yet."
"And you invited us here because you think the problem is that we're assuming time exists."
Barbarian picked up a cup of tea.
"I invited you here because I think you are assuming that time is something more than the relationships between events."
"No. It's a question designed to make the answer complicated."
Derek looked at the clock on the wall.
"That's at least a useful operational definition."

"Clocks measure regular physical processes. Oscillations. Rotations. Atomic transitions. Mechanical motion. You choose a process you believe is sufficiently regular, call it a clock, and compare other changes with it."
"So a clock doesn't measure some invisible substance called time."
"No. It means we have to be careful about what we mean by 'exists.'"
He put an apple on the table.
"Do we need time to describe that?"
"We need to distinguish the first state from the second."
"But suppose instead of saying the apple moved through time, we simply describe two complete configurations."
"The relationship between them tells us that the apple changed position."
"And the amount of change tells us something about the dynamics."
Penny Gent looked at the clocks.
"So you're saying that reality consists of configurations, and what we call time is the ordering or relationship between them."
"But General Relativity doesn't give us such an easy picture."
"In General Relativity, time is part of spacetime."
"And the geometry of spacetime is dynamical."
"Proper time along a worldline is measurable."
"An observer carries a clock, and the clock measures proper time along that observer's worldline."
"So we cannot simply declare time nonexistent and walk away."
"I have a much more irritating plan."
"General Relativity tells us something extraordinary. There is no single universal time that everyone in the universe must agree upon."
"In General Relativity, the situation becomes even richer because spacetime itself is dynamical."
"So the universe doesn't come with a giant clock mounted above it."
Trevor looked at the clock shelf.
"Then what are clocks actually telling us?"
"We've been here ten minutes and you're already using our phrase."
Penny Gent pointed toward the shelf.
"But you remarked that they don't measure time."
"I remarked that they don't measure a substance called time."
He picked up an old railway watch.

"This tells you how one physical process relates to another. If you synchronize two clocks under specified conditions, move them apart, accelerate one, place them at different gravitational potentials and compare them again, the difference tells you something about spacetime."
Derek looked at the brass clock Trevor was holding.
He placed the clock on the table.
"Which means either you saw it before it arrived here..."
"...or the clock has somehow moved backwards through whatever we mean by time."
"This is precisely why I wanted to speak to you."
"Because you understand the mathematics well enough not to be frightened by the philosophical consequences."
"Suppose we forget the word 'time' for a moment."
"Each event has relationships to other events."
"Some observers call one relationship earlier and another later."
"And the Lorentz transformation tells us how different inertial observers assign coordinates to events."
"While General Relativity tells us how the geometry of spacetime behaves in the presence of matter and energy."
"And proper time is what a physical clock measures along a worldline."
"So perhaps what we're calling time is the structure of these relationships."
"That is a respectable way of putting it."
"And if the strange clocks aren't showing different amounts of some universal substance called time..."
"We still don't know why the relationships are wrong."
"Because I want to show you something."
They followed him through the back door.
The garden was larger than Derek had expected.
There was a lawn, a small pond, several trees and a stone path.
At the far end stood a tall wooden post.
At the top was a clock.
"This one is synchronized with the one inside."
"Same gravitational potential to a very good approximation."
A bird landed on the fence.
A car passed somewhere beyond the garden.
Then the clock on the post stopped.
The clock had stopped at exactly 11:17:00.
But it was moving in tiny jumps.
He looked at the clock inside the house.
A bird flew across the garden.
The clock in the photograph showed 11:03:17.
He looked at the actual clocks.
Weinstein was staring at the sky.
The bird was suspended in the air.
"Because I know what you're going to say."
He stared at the suspended plane.
The surface of the water was perfectly still.
But a small insect was sitting on it.
"You've been waiting your entire career to say that, haven't you?"
"If time has stopped, why are we moving?"
"Because our local physical processes haven't stopped."
"Because you're trying to make the word 'time' do too much work."
"Suppose there is no fundamental time variable ticking behind reality."
He pointed to the frozen plane.
"One configuration contains that plane in one position."
"The clocks are physical systems within those configurations."
"So if we move from one configuration to another while the clocks don't advance, the clocks don't provide the ordering."
"But then what has happened to the time coordinate in the equations?"
"Then you aren't denying time in physics."
"I'm denying that the symbol t must correspond to a fundamental substance flowing through the universe."
Penny Gent looked at the frozen plane.
"So what we're seeing is a physical configuration in which the clocks aren't advancing."
"They're just one type of physical process."
Derek looked at the brass clock.
"And this one is somehow associated with a different sequence of configurations."
"That the clock isn't measuring some universal time."
"And that physical process can disagree with other physical processes."
"Which is exactly what relativity already told us."
"Because in ordinary relativity, the clocks disagree according to the geometry of spacetime."
Weinstein pointed at the frozen garden.
"We have no idea what geometry we're dealing with."
The plane continued across the sky.
All the clocks began ticking again.
Derek looked at the wall clock through the window.
Derek looked at the photograph again.
Then he noticed something he hadn't noticed before.
It had been hidden beneath the fold.
Penny Gent looked at the paper.
The brass clock in Derek's pocket began ticking.
"Do you still think time doesn't exist?"
"I think reality is perfectly capable of existing without asking my permission."
"Time may be a very useful description of relationships between events."
"But I have never been convinced that the universe itself carries a watch."
Derek put the clock back into his pocket.
Derek looked toward the frozen sky.
"We have forty-seven minutes to find out where the train is going."
"You have forty-seven minutes to find out where the train has already been."

By now you have encountered clocks that disagree, trains that arrive before they leave, corridors that acquire extra doors, rain that occasionally develops opinions, cucumbers, holograms, singularities, dolphins, and a man who apparently exists in more than one place.
You may reasonably be wondering whether any of this has anything whatsoever to do with physics.
Annoyingly, quite a lot of it does.
The purpose of this appendix is not merely to tell you what the characters were talking about. It is to leave you able to explain the central ideas yourself.
Each chapter therefore does four things.
First, it states the idea in ordinary language.
Second, it gives you the physics underneath the joke.
Third, it points out the most tempting way to misunderstand it.
Fourth, it gives you a tiny test. If you can answer that test, you have learned something rather than merely survived it.
You do not need university-level mathematics to understand the central ideas.
A willingness to tolerate letters standing for things.
And the ability to accept that the universe does not care what you personally think "obviously" means.
One useful rule will appear repeatedly: separate what an observer measures from what the theory requires is invariant.
Another is even more important: when a metaphor helps you understand the physics, keep the metaphor. When the metaphor starts making predictions, throw it away.
The cucumber, for example, is an excellent teacher.
It is not a peer-reviewed vegetable.

The holographic principle arose from thinking about black-hole entropy.
Black holes have an entropy proportional to the area of their event horizon, not simply the volume inside.
Perhaps the information describing a region of space can be encoded on its boundary.
In certain theories, this idea becomes mathematically precise — but not as a general statement that our universe is literally a hologram.
The most famous example is AdS/CFT duality, associated especially with Juan Maldacena.
A gravitational theory in a higher-dimensional spacetime can be equivalent to a quantum field theory without gravity living on a lower-dimensional boundary.
This does not mean the universe is literally a two-dimensional cinema screen.
It means that two apparently different mathematical descriptions can encode the same underlying physics.
And that connects beautifully with relativity.
In Special Relativity, different observers use different coordinates.
In General Relativity, different coordinate systems can describe the same geometry.
In holographic duality, dramatically different-looking theories can describe the same physical system.
A description is not necessarily the same thing as the underlying physical system it describes.

Now for the actual physics, which Penny Gent gets right and the poster does not.
First, the disclaimer Penny Gent makes herself: the film's multiverse is not the multiverse that occasionally shows up in serious physics.

Real physicists do debate a handful of multiverse-shaped ideas — different interpretations of quantum mechanics, different regions produced by an early, rapidly expanding universe, that sort of thing.
None of them look remotely like a laundromat, and you do not need to know a single one of their names to follow this chapter.

The film is a storytelling device, not a scientific interpretation of quantum mechanics. Treat it exactly the way you would treat the cucumber: an excellent aid to intuition and completely inadmissible as evidence.
What the film is quietly useful for is an idea this book has been building since Chapter 2. It doesn't need a single equation.
Physics is not tied to one particular coordinate description. What matters is the physical content that different valid descriptions predict and, where appropriate, the quantities that are invariant.
Say the same true sentence in English and in German.
The words are completely different. The grammar is completely different.
What the sentence means has not changed at all.
In physics, an observable is a quantity associated with a possible measurement. It is not simply whatever survives a change of coordinates — Penny is simplifying things rather enthusiastically.
The coordinates may be different; the physical prediction is not.
You have already watched this happen twice, in plainer clothes.
In Chapter 2, two observers disagreed about distances, durations, even which of two events happened first — yet agreed on one particular combination of those numbers, the invariant interval.
Different measuring sticks. Same underlying fact.

In Chapter 11, we meet a particularly striking example from theoretical physics: in the AdS/CFT correspondence, a gravitational theory in a higher-dimensional spacetime can be mathematically equivalent to a quantum field theory without gravity on a lower-dimensional boundary. Two descriptions that look almost nothing alike, yet encode the same physics.
It is a bit like Weinstein filing his patent notes in German and Trevor filing the same conclusions in English. Argue about the language all you like — the invention still works.
Penny Gent's contribution, from row F, is to notice the pattern and ask the next obvious question.
If measuring sticks and entire mathematical languages are optional, what about a person's own life story?
A “worldline” is the technical term for an object's path through spacetime — in the human case, its physical history.
If that history is only one way of describing some deeper underlying state, then the story you tell about yourself may be exactly as optional as which ruler you used.
This is why she texts Derek to stop investigating the clocks and start investigating the descriptions.

Without quite meaning to, she has beaten Sherlock the dolphin to the punch. His idea, delivered properly in Chapter 15, is that spacetime itself — and maybe even the order events happen in — might emerge from relationships, rather than being the stage those relationships happen on.
And here is why this chapter earns its place directly before the tensors.

A tensor exists purely to solve the problem Penny Gent has just described: a mathematical object whose components are allowed to look totally different depending on your point of view, as long as the underlying thing they describe never changes.
As Chapter 15 puts it, a tensor is what happens when a vector gets promoted and starts having opinions about several directions at once.
Which is, roughly, what just happened to Penny Gent.
What the reader should take away:
1. A film multiverse is a metaphor, nothing more — do not cite Marvel in an exam.
2. The idea actually worth keeping: rulers, languages, coordinate systems, and maybe even life stories, can all be different descriptions of one and the same underlying reality.
3. An “observable” is simply whatever survives the translation — the one thing every honest description has to agree on.
4. This is exactly why, three chapters from now, General Relativity needs tensors: they are built specifically to say the same thing in every language.
Jamie Lee Curtis, in accordance with the previously established Law of Conservation of Actresses, once again survives.

This is where relativity becomes particularly dangerous for ordinary English.
The train appears, in one description, to arrive before it leaves.
That sounds like a violation of causality.
But before screaming "time machine", we need to distinguish coordinate descriptions from actual causal structure.
In relativity, different observers can disagree about the temporal ordering of spacelike-separated events.
For causally connected events, all inertial observers agree on their temporal order. Relativity does not let an ordinary cause arrive after its effect merely by changing coordinates.
The light cone is the key.

The light-cone structure — what can causally influence what — is invariant.
So if Derek sees something that appears to happen before its cause, we should first ask:
Are those events actually causally connected?
If not, the apparent reversal may simply be a consequence of the coordinate system.
If they are causally connected and the story really reverses their order, then we have left ordinary Special Relativity and need some additional physics — or a very good explanation from the Bureau.
At which point Derek should probably stop buying train tickets.

But before we explain that equation, we need to meet the things lurking inside it.
Tensors — Vectors' Slightly More Ambitious Cousins
A vector is already rather clever.
It can tell you something like:
"Go three metres east and two metres north."
It has components, and those components change when you change coordinates, but the underlying vector itself is the same physical thing.
A tensor takes this idea one step further.
At an introductory level, you can think of a tensor as a mathematical object that describes relationships between several directions at once.
Vector: a quantity with directional components.
Tensor: a quantity whose components describe relationships between directions.
So, in the spirit of the Bureau:
A tensor is what happens when a vector gets promoted and starts having opinions about several directions simultaneously.
It is not the formal mathematical definition.

A tensor is not simply a "higher-dimensional vector." What matters is that its components obey specific transformation rules when we change coordinates, so that the underlying physical object remains well-defined.
And that is exactly why tensors are so useful in General Relativity.
Someone can be falling into a black hole while someone else is sitting safely in an office complaining about the coffee.
We need mathematical objects that behave properly when we change coordinates.
The most important tensor to meet first is the metric tensor, written:
It tells us how spacetime is measured.

Don't let the Greek letters intimidate you.
"Combine the changes in all the relevant directions according to the metric, and you get the spacetime interval."
The metric is therefore rather like the instruction manual for measuring spacetime.

Once you know the metric, an enormous amount of physics follows.
It describes the distribution and flow of physical quantities such as:
and energy and momentum flowing through spacetime.
You can think of it as an extraordinarily sophisticated inventory of what matter and energy are doing.
Trevor once called it "the universe's spreadsheet."
He did, however, admit that the analogy wasn't completely useless.
Then things become progressively more tensorish.
The Riemann curvature tensor contains the full local information about spacetime curvature.
The Ricci tensor packages an important part of that curvature.
And the Einstein tensor, (Gμν), packages the relevant curvature information in precisely the form required by Einstein's field equation.
There is a reason physicists need all these objects.
Curvature is not adequately described by saying:
"Space is a bit bent over there."
That would be charming but mathematically inadequate.
It can differ in different directions.
It can affect neighbouring paths differently.
Tensors are the machinery that lets us describe all of this without losing the physics every time somebody changes coordinates.
And now, finally, we can look at the equation.
The right-hand side is matter and energy.
The Einstein field equation therefore remarks, in gloriously compressed mathematical form:
The geometry of spacetime is related to the distribution of matter and energy.
Or, as Derek would put it:
"Matter tells spacetime how to curve, and spacetime tells matter how to behave."
And for once, he would be right.
But Is General Relativity the Final Answer?
But it does not appear to provide the complete description of nature at the quantum level.
Black-hole singularities and the earliest moments of the universe are obvious warning signs.
This is where quantum gravity enters.

If a deeper theory eventually explains this, General Relativity would not become "wrong."
It would become something like thermodynamics.
Neither is a fundamental microscopic object.
And this brings us back to Weinstein's original problem.
Perhaps the final theory does not replace General Relativity.
Perhaps it would explain why General Relativity works so remarkably well.
That would be a considerably more interesting achievement.

Or you can have another piece of cake.

The question that has been lurking underneath the entire book:
If space and time can be observer-dependent, if gravity is geometry, if geometry might itself emerge from deeper physics, and if different descriptions can encode the same reality...
